extracted.intended_audience: practitioners representing clients before the USPTO (registered patent attorneys, patent agents, law firms practicing patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (duties, prohibitions, recordkeeping, withdrawal/sale rules, communications, and related supervisory responsibilities) governing practitioners who represent clients before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing an organization — duties and disclosure when constituents violate law
rubrics_metrics.description: When representing an organization, if a constituent's action or refusal to act is a violation of a legal obligation to the organization or a violation of law likely to result in substantial injury, the practitioner shall proceed as is reasonably necessary in the organization's best interest, refer the matter to higher authority, and, if the highest authority fails to address a clear violation that is reasonably certain to result in substantial injury, may reveal information relating to the representation to the extent reasonably necessary to prevent substantial injury (subject to exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must refer the matter to higher authority (including highest authority able to act). Disclosure under this rule is permitted only if the practitioner reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent substantial injury and is subject to exception when the representation is to investigate an alleged violation or to defend the organization/constituent against a claim arising from the alleged violation. If discharged or if withdrawing under circumstances that permit action under these paragraphs, the practitioner must take steps reasonably necessary to assure the organization's highest authority is informed of the discharge or withdrawal. When dealing with constituents whose interests are adverse to the organization, the practitioner shall explain the identity of the client. Dual representation of organization constituents is allowed subject to § 11.107; required consent must be given by an appropriate official other than the individual represented or by shareholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client with diminished capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a client's capacity to make adequately considered decisions is diminished, the practitioner shall, as far as reasonably possible, maintain a normal client-practitioner relationship and may take reasonably necessary protective action if the client is at risk of substantial harm and cannot act in the client's own interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protective actions may include consulting individuals or entities able to take protective action and, when appropriate, seeking appointment of guardian ad litem, conservator or guardian. Information relating to representation is protected under § 11.106 but the practitioner is impliedly authorized to reveal information to the extent reasonably necessary to protect the client's interests when taking protective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safekeeping client and third-party property
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall hold client or third-person property separate from the practitioner's own property; funds must be kept in a separate account in the state where the practitioner's office is situated (or elsewhere with client/third-person consent). Complete records must be kept and preserved for five years after termination of the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other property must be identified and safeguarded. Practitioner may deposit own funds in a client trust account only to pay bank service charges and only in the amount necessary. Advance legal fees and expenses paid must be deposited into a client trust account and withdrawn only as fees are earned or expenses incurred. Upon receiving funds or property in which a client/third person has an interest, promptly notify the client/third person and promptly deliver any funds/property they are entitled to receive; upon request render a full accounting. When multiple persons claim interests in property, keep property separate until dispute resolved and promptly distribute undisputed portions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required client trust account records
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must maintain specified records for separate client/third-person accounts, including receipt/disbursement journals, ledger records, copies of retainer/compensation agreements, accountings, bills, disbursement records, checkbook registers and bank records, records of electronic transfers, trial balances and reconciliations, and related portions of client files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ledger records must show, for each client/beneficiary, source of funds, names of persons for whom funds were held, amounts, descriptions and amounts of charges/withdrawals, and payees. Records of electronic transfers must include authorizer, date, recipient, confirmation from financial institution including trust account number and time/date of transfer. Monthly trial balances and quarterly reconciliations required. Copies of portions of client files reasonably related to trust transactions must be kept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client trust account safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate client accounts must be safeguarded: only a practitioner or person under the direct supervision of the practitioner may be an authorized signatory or authorize transfers; receipts shall be deposited intact and with sufficient detail; withdrawals only by check payable to a named payee (not to cash) or by authorized electronic transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records of deposit should identify each item. These safeguards apply to all separate accounts for clients or third persons kept by a practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format, availability, and equivalency of records
rubrics_metrics.description: Required records may be maintained electronically, photographically, or by other media provided they comply with recordkeeping requirements and printed copies can be produced; records must be readily accessible to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records kept by a lawyer are deemed compliant if they meet the recordkeeping requirements of a state where the lawyer is licensed and in good standing, or where the principal place of business is located, or the requirements of this section. Records for law firms employing registered patent agents or limited-recognition persons in the U.S. are deemed compliant if they meet the recordkeeping requirements of an applicable state or this section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory withdrawal or refusal to represent
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not represent, or shall withdraw from representing, a client if the representation will result in violation of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct or other law, the practitioner's physical or mental condition materially impairs ability to represent the client, or the practitioner is discharged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are mandatory grounds for declining or terminating representation except as stated in paragraph (c) about tribunal notice/permission requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissive withdrawal grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may withdraw from representation under specified circumstances, including withdrawal without material adverse effect on client interests; client persists in criminal/fraudulent course of action; client used the practitioner's services to perpetrate crime/fraud; client insists on repugnant action; client substantially fails to fulfill an obligation after reasonable warning; representation imposes unreasonable financial burden or has been rendered unreasonably difficult; or other good cause exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal is permitted when it can be accomplished without material adverse effect or for other enumerated good causes; practitioner must still comply with tribunal rules about notice/permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal notice and steps upon termination
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must comply with applicable law requiring notice to or permission of a tribunal when terminating representation; when ordered to continue representation, the practitioner shall do so. Upon termination, the practitioner shall take steps reasonably practicable to protect the client's interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protective steps include giving reasonable notice to the client, allowing time to retain other counsel, surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled, and refunding any advanced payment of fee or expense that has not been earned or incurred. Practitioner may retain papers to the extent permitted by other law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of law practice — conditions and client notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner or law firm may sell or purchase a law practice or an area of law practice including goodwill if specified conditions are met: seller ceases practice in the geographic area, the entire practice or area of practice is sold to one or more lawyers (with special rule for USPTO patent practice), and clients receive written notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practice involving patent proceedings before the Office, sale may be only to one or more registered practitioners. Seller must give written notice to each client including proposed sale, client's right to retain other counsel or take possession of file, and that client consent to transfer will be presumed if no objection within 90 days. If a client cannot be given notice, transfer may occur only upon a court order authorizing transfer; in-camera disclosure to court limited to necessary information. Fees charged clients shall not be increased by reason of the sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties to prospective clients — confidentiality and disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who has learned information from a prospective client shall not use or reveal that information (except as § 11.109 would permit for information of a former client) and shall not represent a client with interests materially adverse to those of a prospective client in the same or a substantially related matter if the practitioner received information that could be significantly harmful to the prospective client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation is permissible despite disqualifying information if both affected client and prospective client give informed consent confirmed in writing; or if the disqualified practitioner took reasonable measures to avoid additional exposure, is timely screened from participation and apportioned no part of the fee, and written notice is promptly given to the prospective client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisor role — independent judgment and candid advice
rubrics_metrics.description: In representing a client, a practitioner shall exercise independent professional judgment and render candid advice, potentially referring to legal and non-legal considerations (moral, economic, social, political) relevant to the client's situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisory role permits consideration of broader factors beyond strict legal analysis when rendering advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluations for use by third persons
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may provide an evaluation of a matter affecting a client for use by someone other than the client if the practitioner reasonably believes making the evaluation is compatible with other aspects of the practitioner-client relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the evaluation is likely to affect the client's interests materially and adversely, the practitioner shall not provide the evaluation unless the client gives informed consent. Except as authorized in connection with a report of an evaluation, information relating to the evaluation is protected by § 11.106.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner serving as third-party neutral
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner serving as a third-party neutral (e.g., arbitrator or mediator) must inform unrepresented parties that the practitioner is not representing them and, when necessary, explain the difference between the neutral role and an advocate's role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party neutral duties include explaining lack of representation and ensuring unrepresented persons understand the practitioner's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meritorious claims and contentions
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not bring or defend a proceeding, or assert or controvert an issue therein, unless there is a basis in law and fact that is not frivolous; this includes good-faith arguments for extension, modification, or reversal of existing law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must ensure claims and contentions have factual and legal support and may argue for changes in law in good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expediting proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall make reasonable efforts to expedite proceedings before a tribunal consistent with the interests of the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must balance speed with client's interests while avoiding unnecessary delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly make false statements of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct previously made false statements; must disclose controlling adverse authority in inter partes proceedings (and in ex parte proceedings before the Office if not otherwise disclosed); shall not offer evidence the practitioner knows to be false and must take reasonable remedial measures if falsity is discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner who knows of criminal/fraudulent conduct related to a proceeding must take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the tribunal if necessary. Duties continue to conclusion of the proceeding even if disclosure requires revealing information otherwise protected by § 11.106. In ex parte proceedings, must inform tribunal of all material facts known to enable informed decision. In Office proceedings, disclose information necessary to comply with duty-of-disclosure provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness to opposing party and counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall not unlawfully obstruct access to evidence or alter/destroy/conceal material having evidentiary value; shall not falsify evidence or counsel a witness to testify falsely; shall not knowingly disobey tribunal rules (except open refusal asserting no valid obligation exists); shall not make frivolous discovery requests or fail to comply with proper discovery; and shall avoid irrelevant or unsupported allusions or personal opinions about matters in the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner shall not request a person other than a client to refrain from voluntarily giving relevant information to another party except when the person is a relative, employee, or agent of a client and the practitioner reasonably believes the person's interests will not be adversely affected by refraining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and decorum of the tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not seek to influence judges, hearing officers, jurors, Office employees, or other officials by means prohibited by law; shall not communicate ex parte with such persons during the proceeding unless authorized; and shall not engage in conduct intended to disrupt any proceeding before a tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes prohibition on improper contacts and disruptive behavior; paragraph (c) reserved in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial publicity restrictions and narrow exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who participates in litigation shall not make extrajudicial statements that the practitioner knows or reasonably should know will be disseminated and will have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing an adjudicative proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted statements include identification of claim/offense/defense and persons involved (except when prohibited), information in a public record, that an investigation is in progress, scheduling/results of steps in litigation, requests for assistance obtaining evidence, and warnings of danger when there is reason to believe substantial harm may occur. Practitioner may make limited statements reasonably believed necessary to protect client from substantial undue prejudicial effect of recent publicity not initiated by practitioner or client. No practitioner associated in a firm/agency with a practitioner subject to the prohibition may make a prohibited statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner as witness
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not act as advocate in a proceeding before a tribunal in which the practitioner is likely to be a necessary witness unless (1) the testimony relates to an uncontested issue, (2) the testimony relates to the nature and value of legal services rendered, or (3) disqualification would work substantial hardship on the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner may act as advocate where another practitioner in the firm is likely to be called as a witness unless precluded by §§ 11.107 or 11.109.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate in nonadjudicative proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner representing a client before a legislative body or administrative agency in a nonadjudicative proceeding shall disclose that the appearance is in a representative capacity and shall conform to the provisions of §§ 11.303(a)-(c), 11.304(a)-(c), and 11.305.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonadjudicative advocacy requires disclosure of representative capacity and adherence to candor, fairness, and impartiality rules referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness in statements to others
rubrics_metrics.description: In representing a client, a practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of material fact or law to a third person, nor fail to disclose a material fact to a third person when disclosure is necessary to avoid assisting a criminal or fraudulent act by a client, unless disclosure is prohibited by § 11.106.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to communications with third parties outside tribunal proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication with person represented by counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not communicate about the subject of the representation with a person the practitioner knows to be represented by another practitioner in the matter, unless the practitioner has the consent of the other practitioner or is authorized by law, rule, or court order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: communications with government officials who are represented by counsel but have authority to redress grievances are allowed provided the practitioner discloses identity and that the practitioner represents a party with a claim against the government when the communication relates to a matter for which the official is represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with unrepresented persons
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with an unrepresented person on behalf of a client, a practitioner shall not state or imply that the practitioner is disinterested, shall correct misunderstandings about the practitioner's role, and shall not give legal advice to the unrepresented person other than advising them to secure counsel if the person's interests have or may have a reasonable possibility of being in conflict with the client's interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must ensure the unrepresented person understands the practitioner's representative role and avoid creating the impression of impartiality when representing a client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for rights of third persons
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not use means that have no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay, or burden a third person, nor use methods of obtaining evidence that violate that person's legal rights. A practitioner who receives a document or electronically stored information that was inadvertently sent shall promptly notify the sender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers lawful, respectful investigative and litigation methods and prompt notification obligations for inadvertent disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities of partners, managers, and supervisory practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Partners and practitioners with comparable managerial authority must make reasonable efforts to ensure the firm has measures giving reasonable assurance that all practitioners conform to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct. Supervisors must make reasonable efforts to ensure those they supervise conform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner is responsible for another practitioner's violation if the practitioner ordered or ratified the conduct, or is a partner/manager or supervisory practitioner who knew of the conduct when its consequences could be avoided or mitigated and failed to take reasonable remedial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities of subordinate practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: A subordinate practitioner is bound by the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct even when acting at another's direction, but does not violate the rules if acting in accordance with a supervisory practitioner's reasonable resolution of an arguable question of professional duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subordinate practitioners must follow rules but reasonable supervisory directions on arguable questions of duty can shield them from violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities regarding non-practitioner assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners with managerial authority must make reasonable efforts to ensure that non-practitioner assistants' conduct is compatible with the practitioner's professional obligations; supervisors must similarly ensure conformity. A practitioner is responsible for a non-practitioner’s conduct that would be a violation by a practitioner if the practitioner ordered or ratified the conduct or, having managerial/supervisory authority, knew of the conduct when its consequences could be avoided or mitigated and failed to take reasonable remedial action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to employees or retained non-practitioner assistants and requires reasonable oversight and remedial action when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional independence of a practitioner — fee-sharing and practice structures
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner or law firm shall not share legal fees with a non-practitioner except in limited circumstances (payment to estate, purchase price pursuant to § 11.117, inclusion of non-practitioner employees in compensation/retirement plans, or sharing fees with qualifying 501(c)(3) organizations). A practitioner shall not form a partnership with a non-practitioner if any activities of the partnership consist of the practice of law, nor permit a person who recommends/employs/pays the practitioner to direct or regulate the practitioner's professional judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions are narrowly defined. Prohibitions on non-practitioner ownership or managerial control subject to paragraph (e) exception where arrangements fully comply with applicable state licensing laws, rules, and regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized practice of law
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of that jurisdiction's regulation of the legal profession, nor assist another in doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must be mindful of jurisdictional licensing and practice restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on right to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not participate in offering or making agreements that restrict the right of a practitioner to practice after termination of the relationship, except agreements concerning benefits upon retirement; and shall not participate in agreements in which such a restriction is part of a settlement of a client controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibition is intended to preserve practitioners' post-termination practice freedom except for limited retirement benefit arrangements and does not bar legitimate practice transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities regarding law-related services
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner is subject to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct with respect to law-related services if the services are provided by the practitioner in circumstances not distinct from provision of legal services, or by an entity controlled by the practitioner if the practitioner fails to take reasonable measures to assure that the person obtaining the services knows they are not legal services and that client-practitioner protections do not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must ensure appropriate disclosures and separations when providing law-related or nonlegal services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications concerning a practitioner's services — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not make a false or misleading communication about the practitioner or the practitioner's services; a communication is false or misleading if it contains a material misrepresentation of fact or law or omits a fact necessary to make the statement as a whole not materially misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to all advertising, marketing, and public communications; practitioner must ensure accuracy and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications concerning services — specific compensation and certification rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may communicate regarding services through any medium but shall not compensate a person for recommending the practitioner's services except for enumerated exceptions (pay reasonable advertising costs, pay usual charges of legal service plan/referral service, pay for law practice purchase per § 11.117, non-exclusive reciprocal referral agreements with client informed, give nominal appreciation gifts). A practitioner shall not state or imply certification as a specialist unless certified by an approved or accredited organization and the certifying organization's name is disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal referral agreements must be non-exclusive and clients must be informed of the existence and nature of the agreement. Nominal gifts are allowed if not intended or expected as compensation for recommendations. Certification claims must be truthful and identify certifying body when allowed.
